mappings.note: Line parallel to the time axis on a position-time graph means the object is at rest. A state of motion read from graph shape, so LO-1's interpret clause rather than LO-2's slope-to-quantity operation.
Significance of the area under a velocity-time graph: displacement. LO-2 verbatim; the answer names a kinematic quantity, which is the discriminator against the LO-1 graph items.
States what v=u+at relates. Knowledge of the equation set, which belongs with LO-3; LO-4 is reserved for items that substitute values, and none are supplied.
Write s=ut+(1/2)at^2. Same equation-recall demand as V82, distinguished only by which of the three equations is wanted; both honestly share LO-3.
Corrects the claim that the equations work for any accelerated motion. The constant-acceleration restriction is a property of the derivation, so LO-3 rather than LO-4.
Definition of uniform circular motion - named explicitly in LO-1. C-8.1-LO-2 is withheld because no speed expression is asked for, which is exactly what separates this item from V88.

Why uniform circular motion is accelerated. LO-1's definitions of acceleration and of uniform circular motion together; the chapter asks this same question at five difficulty levels and they share this outcome honestly.
Direction of velocity in uniform circular motion is along the tangent - definitional (LO-1). No prediction is asked, so unlike O58 and V92 it does not take LO-60.

Asks for the 2(pi)r/T formula itself. The only outcome in the frame covering the speed expression for circular motion, which separates this cleanly from the LO-1 conceptual circular-motion items around it.
Displacement after one full round is zero. The distance/displacement contrast on a closed path (LO-1); no speed expression required, so not C-8.1-LO-2.

POOR FIT. The answer is the name of an ancient text. Mapped to LO-1 because the concept credited to it is the definition of speed, but the recall target itself has no home in this frame - same finding as its O15 twin.
Instantaneous versus average velocity. LO-1 defines velocity and is the only outcome that could host this, though note that no outcome in this frame names instantaneous velocity - a mild gap.

What would happen if the ring were lifted: a prediction about the outcome of an activity (LO-60), answered by the tangential-velocity definition (LO-1). It splits from S107 below, which asks the student to describe the activity rather than predict its result.

POOR FIT. An example of two-dimensional motion. Both LO-1 and its parent competency are scoped to one dimension, so nothing in the frame covers this; LO-1 is cited as the nearest definitional home. Same finding as O63.
Slope of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration - LO-2's 'average acceleration from velocity-time graph' clause. A quantity, not a state of motion, so not LO-1.

POOR FIT. Asks the scientific term for the acceleration caused by gravity. No learning outcome mentions gravity; the parent competency C2.1 names 'acceleration due to gravity' explicitly, so the competency is the only legitimate home and is cited alone.
Explain with an example how displacement can be zero while distance is not. LO-1's differentiation clause, asked for as an explanation with an illustration rather than as a calculation.

Zero average velocity with non-zero average speed, with a daily-life example. The speed/velocity half of LO-1's differentiation, distinct from S96's distance/displacement half by which pair of quantities is contrasted.

Definition of average acceleration plus its SI unit plus the condition for it to oppose motion. All three parts sit in LO-1 (define, express in SI units, direction in straight-line motion); nothing is calculated.
Genuinely two demands: draw the position-time graph for constant velocity (LO-1's plot clause) and then obtain the velocity from its slope (LO-2). Neither code alone covers the item.
How to get displacement from a velocity-time graph under constant acceleration (trapezium area). Pure LO-2; no graph has to be drawn from scratch, so C8.1 is not added as it is for N14 and N15.
Same two-demand shape as S99 but on the velocity-time axis: draw the graph for uniform retardation (LO-1) and interpret its slope as acceleration (LO-2).
How graph shape distinguishes stationary, constant-velocity and changing-velocity motion. Every answer is a state of motion, which is the discriminator that keeps this on LO-1 and off LO-2.
State all three kinematic equations and what each symbol means. The equation set as a whole, so LO-3; LO-4 would need values to substitute and none are given.

Draw an athlete on a circular track and explain how the velocity direction changes. Definitional content about uniform circular motion (LO-1); no 2(pi)R/T expression is required, so C-8.1-LO-2 is withheld.
